title: Preheater

introduction.definition: A preheater heats a fluid before it enters the main process, recovering heat that would otherwise be lost. In a closed feedwater heater, steam extracted from a turbine condenses on the outside of U-tubes and heats boiler feedwater flowing inside. The condensate collects at the bottom (drain-cooling zone) and drains to the next heater.
applications: Boiler feedwater heaters (LP/HP) in power plants
Combustion air or fuel oil preheating
key_points: Raises the temperature of the incoming fluid using waste or bled heat
Shell side condenses steam at near-constant temperature
Each feedwater heater stage improves Rankine cycle efficiency
Impingement plate protects tubes at steam inlet
introduction.summary: A preheater raises the temperature of a fluid before it enters the main process — for example a feedwater heater, where turbine extraction steam condenses on the outside of a U-tube bundle and heats the boiler feedwater flowing inside. This recovers heat and improves cycle efficiency.

working_principle.characteristic_curve: Terminal temperature difference (TTD = steam sat. T − water outlet T) and drain-cooler approach (DCA) are the main performance indicators.

temperature.title: Temperature: water heats along the bundle
temperature.description: Feedwater (cool, blue) gains heat as it passes the tubes; condensing steam on the shell side stays near its saturation temperature, which is why the temperature difference is largest at the cold end. Condensate is sub-cooled in the drain-cooling zone at the bottom.

foundation: Support on saddles or structure designed for the operating and full-of-water (hydro-test) weight; bolt one saddle and slot the other for thermal expansion.
alignment: Level the unit (or set the specified slope for drainage); leave tube-bundle pull-out space equal to the bundle length.
piping: Connect nozzles without forcing (check allowable nozzle loads); fit vents at high points and drains at low points on both sides.
Steam-heated units: install a steam trap or level-controlled drain and a vacuum breaker so condensate cannot back up.
commissioning: Hydro-test both sides per code; vent air; introduce the cold fluid first, then the hot fluid gradually to avoid thermal shock.

routine.task: Watch TTD, DCA and drain level.

overhaul.task: Inspect tubes (eddy current); plug leaking tubes.

lubrication: No lubrication for the static parts — lubricate valve stems, rotating parts and drives per maker.

symptoms: Rising drain level, high drain flow
causes: Erosion at steam inlet, vibration, corrosion

safety: Protect against tube rupture overpressure of the shell; never isolate the shell relief path.

script.narration: This module introduces the Preheater.
A preheater heats a fluid before it enters the main process, recovering heat that would otherwise be lost.
In a closed feedwater heater, steam extracted from a turbine condenses on the outside of U-tubes and heats boiler feedwater flowing inside.
The condensate collects at the bottom (drain-cooling zone) and drains to the next heater.
Typical applications include boiler feedwater heaters (LP/HP) in power plants; crude and process feed preheating; combustion air or fuel oil preheating.

script.narration: How the Preheater works.
Feedwater enters the channel and flows through the U-tubes.
Steam enters the shell; an impingement plate protects the tubes.
Steam condenses on the tubes, giving its latent heat to the water.
Condensate collects and is drained under level control.
Heated feedwater leaves through the channel outlet.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.
Feedwater (cool, blue) gains heat as it passes the tubes; condensing steam on the shell side stays near its saturation temperature, which is why the temperature difference is largest at the cold end.

video_tutorials.title: Preheater — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Preheater.
Watch TTD, DCA and drain level.
Check vent operation (non-condensables).
Inspect tubes (eddy current); plug leaking tubes.
Watch for tube leak: rising drain level, high drain flow. Common cause: erosion at steam inlet, vibration, corrosion.
Watch for high TTD: lower outlet temperature. Common cause: air blanketing (vent blocked), fouling.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
